question: A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules, is wanted after one last conversion — but it starts with two speed readings. Two speeds of 4 m/s and 11 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 4; from this figure, 7 m/s is subtracted, then 25 m/s is added back. This net speed belongs to an 11 kg slider. A separate thermometer reads 28°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 4, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A machine's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a final subtraction of 2 kN, is the goal — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings of 7 m/s² and 8 m/s² are added and the sum multiplied by 3, giving the effective acceleration. This acts on a 183 kg part, producing a force that is converted into kilonewtons, then reduced by 10 kN. A separate voltmeter reads 5 V, unrelated to this task. The total is scaled by a factor of 5, and finally reduced by 2 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a final addition of 29 N, is wanted — but it starts with a position trace. A part's position follows x(t) = t³ (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous acceleration at t = 2.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on a 41 kg part. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 7, scaled again by 2, then reduced by 7 N, and finally increased by 29 N. What is the final force, in newtons?

On a lab test bench, for each integer k from 1 to 8, a rig logs a reading equal to k; summing all eight readings gives the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 46000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 9, increased by 12 J, converted into kilojoules, and finally reduced by 30 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after two successive deductions, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 10 and multiply to 16; the smaller is kept as the speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 26000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 18 kJ. A separate voltmeter reads 22 V, unrelated to this task. Finally, 23 kJ is subtracted once more. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = t² (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 3 s belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 30000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 10 V, unrelated to this task. The cart's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 10, converted into kilojoules, scaled again by 3, and finally scaled once more by 11. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final doubling, is wanted — but it starts with a batch of test modules. From 6 interchangeable modules, engineers select groups of 3 for a diagnostic test; the number of distinct such groups is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 59000 grams. A separate stopwatch reads 48 seconds, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 5, then increased by 30 kJ, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after two successive adjustments, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 5 and multiply to 6; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is stated as 88000 grams. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 7, converted into kilonewtons, and then reduced by 26 kN. A separate voltmeter reads 20 V, unrelated to this task. Finally, 20 kN is added. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last addition of 24 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = t² + 2t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 1 s and t = 4 s belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 60000 grams. The cart's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 28 kJ, scaled by a factor of 7, and finally increased by 24 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after three successive adjustments, is wanted — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 119 cm and 267 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is found, then multiplied by 6. This total, used as an acceleration in m/s², acts on a part whose mass is 135 kg. To the resulting force, 8 N is added, then 27 N is subtracted, and finally 11 N is subtracted once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a final eightfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 13 and multiply to 40; the smaller is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 163 kg. A separate thermometer reads 34°C, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 4, then increased by 20 kN, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 8. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a vehicle test rig, speed follows v(t) = t³ + 6t² (in m/s, t in seconds); its instantaneous acceleration at t = 3.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on a 2 kg part, producing a force that is scaled by a factor of 5, and scaled again by a factor of 3. A separate voltmeter reads 7 V, unrelated to this task. From the total, 14 N is subtracted, and finally 22 N is subtracted once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules, is the target — reached only after a chain of speed and energy adjustments. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 3t² + 4t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 2 s has 5 m/s added to it. This total speed belongs to a cart whose mass is 20 kg. A separate stopwatch reads 44 seconds, unrelated to this task. The cart's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 7, and finally reduced by 16 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two rods measure 241 cm and 129 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is found, and 10 is added to that number. This total, used as an acceleration in m/s², acts on a part whose mass is 86 kg. A separate voltmeter reads 12 V, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 3, then reduced by 1 N, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 5. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in joules after a final subtraction of 10 J, is wanted — but it starts with a sensor signal. On a test bench, a calibration probe outputs a signal s(t) = 2t³ − 3t² over time t in seconds; the second rate of change of this signal at t = 4.0 s is read directly as a speed, and then 27 m/s is added. This total speed belongs to a 6 kg slider. From the slider's kinetic energy, 23 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 7, and finally 10 J is subtracted. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab's final energy reading, in joules after an elevenfold scaling at the end, is wanted — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 5t² (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 1 s is multiplied by 9. This total speed belongs to a cart whose mass is 32 kg. The cart's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 4, scaled again by 5, and finally scaled once more by 11. What is the final energy, in joules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 4 and multiply to 3; the smaller is kept as the speed of a 46 kg slider. A separate voltmeter reads 18 V, unrelated to this task. From the slider's kinetic energy, 13 J is added, then 14 J is added again, the total is scaled by a factor of 11, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two speeds of 7 m/s and 4 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 3; from this figure, 22 m/s is subtracted, the result is doubled, and 21 m/s is added back. This net speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 28000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 9 V, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 7. What is the final energy, in joules?

On a machine test rig, for each integer k from 1 to 4, a sensor logs a reading equal to 2k − 1; summing all four readings and multiplying by 4 gives the acceleration, in m/s², acting on a part whose mass is stated as 84000 grams. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 7, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 5. What is the final force, in newtons?

Two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 4 and multiply to 3; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a part whose mass is 200 kg. A separate thermometer reads 12°C, unrelated to this task. To the resulting force, 22 N is added, the total is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 12, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 8. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, from 7 interchangeable modules, engineers select groups of 3 for a diagnostic test; the number of distinct such groups is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 33000 grams. From the slider's kinetic energy, 16 J is added, the total is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 12, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 12. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a crane test rig, the rate at which the hook's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 4t² + 7t (in m/s³, t in seconds) from the start of the lift; between t = 0 s and t = 3 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a load whose mass is 85 kg. To the resulting force, 13 N is added, and the total is converted into kilonewtons. A separate pressure gauge reads 50 bar, unrelated to this task. The result is scaled by a factor of 7, and finally 3 kN is added. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + 2t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 2 s and t = 3 s belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 40000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 5 V, unrelated to this task. From the resulting kinetic energy, 2 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 7, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 10 and multiply to 21; the larger is kept as the speed of a 19 kg slider. From the slider's kinetic energy, 11 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 12, then 8 J is subtracted, and finally the result is scaled once more by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in joules?

An engineering team is testing a magnetic rail launcher that fires small research sleds down a horizontal track. During a firing, the sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 3t^2 + 5t, where t is the time in seconds after the coils switch on. The team needs the speed the sled has gained between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, and that speed becomes the release speed of a 14 kilogram sled at the end of the track. (The launch rail itself is 6.0 meters long, a fact that plays no role in what follows.) They need the energy this sled carries because of that release speed, first in joules and then expressed in kilojoules. Taking that kilojoule figure, they multiply it by 11, subtract 13 from the result, and then multiply what remains by 8. What is this final number, in kilojoules?
